```{r}
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(bayesrules)
library(ggformula)
library(broom)
library(patchwork)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
source("notes-helpers.R")

bikes <- bikes |> select(date, season, year, month, weekend, holiday,
                          temp_actual, temp_feel, humidity, windspeed, rides)

bikes_A <- lm(rides ~ temp_actual + windspeed + weekend, data = bikes)
bikes_B <- lm(rides ~ temp_actual + windspeed + weekend + holiday, data = bikes)
bikes_D <- lm(rides ~ temp_actual + windspeed + weekend + holiday + humidity, data = bikes)
bikes_E <- lm(rides ~ temp_actual + windspeed + weekend + holiday + humidity + temp_feel, data = bikes)
bikes_C <- lm(rides ~ temp_feel + humidity + weekend, data = bikes)
n_bikes <- nrow(bikes)
```

`bikes_A` predicts `rides` from `temp_actual`, `windspeed`, and `weekend`.
`bikes_B` adds `holiday`.

```{r}
anova(bikes_A, bikes_B)
```

## Nested models

Two models are **nested** if the reduced model is a ____________________ of the
full model (we get it by setting some $\beta$'s equal to ______).

**Which pairs are nested?** Circle one for each.

| Model 1 | Model 2 | Nested? |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `temp_actual + windspeed` | `temp_actual + windspeed + weekend` | yes / no |
| `temp_actual + weekend` | `temp_feel + weekend` | yes / no |
| `temp_actual + weekend` | `temp_actual * weekend` | yes / no |
| `windspeed + weekend` | `temp_actual + windspeed` | yes / no |

## The extra sums of squares $F$-test

$$F = \frac{(SSE_{reduced} - SSE_{full}) / d}{SSE_{full} / df_{full}}$$

-   Numerator: ______________________________________________
-   Denominator: ______________________________________________
-   A large $F$ means: ______________________________________________

**Example:** Does `holiday` help?

```{r}
#| echo: true
anova(bikes_A, bikes_B)   # reduced model first!
```

With $d = 1$, $F = t^2$. Check: $t$ for `holidayyes` in `bikes_B` is
`r round(summary(bikes_B)$coef["holidayyes", "t value"], 2)`, and
$t^2 =$ `r round(summary(bikes_B)$coef["holidayyes", "t value"]^2, 2)`.

## Adding variables one at a time

```{r}
step_tab <- bind_rows(
  tidy(anova(bikes_A, bikes_B)) |> slice(2) |> mutate(step = "A to B: add holiday"),
  tidy(anova(bikes_B, bikes_D)) |> slice(2) |> mutate(step = "B to D: add humidity"),
  tidy(anova(bikes_D, bikes_E)) |> slice(2) |> mutate(step = "D to E: add temp_feel")
) |>
  mutate(`Delta AIC` = c(AIC(bikes_B) - AIC(bikes_A), AIC(bikes_D) - AIC(bikes_B), AIC(bikes_E) - AIC(bikes_D)),
         `Delta BIC` = c(BIC(bikes_B) - BIC(bikes_A), BIC(bikes_D) - BIC(bikes_B), BIC(bikes_E) - BIC(bikes_D))) |>
  select(step, F = statistic, `p-value` = p.value, `Delta AIC`, `Delta BIC`) |>
  mutate(`p-value` = fmt_p(`p-value`))
knitr::kable(step_tab, digits = 2)
```

*(We'll define AIC and BIC in a few minutes. For now: a negative change
means the bigger model is preferred.)*

`temp_feel` is almost the same variable as `temp_actual`
($r =$ `r round(cor(bikes$temp_actual, bikes$temp_feel), 2)`). What does
the $F$-test say about adding it?

\vspace{.75in}

```{r}
bind_rows(
  tidy(bikes_D) |> filter(term == "temp_actual") |> mutate(model = "D (without temp_feel)"),
  tidy(bikes_E) |> filter(term %in% c("temp_actual", "temp_feel")) |> mutate(model = "E (with temp_feel)")
) |>
  select(model, term, estimate, std.error, p.value) |>
  mutate(p.value = fmt_p(p.value)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

What happened to the standard error of `temp_actual`? Why?

\vspace{.75in}


We need tools that work for *any* two models fit to the same data.

## Adjusted $R^2$

$$R^2_{adj} = 1 - \frac{MSE}{MST}$$

-   can be used for nested **and** non-nested models
-   no formal test or rule for "better enough"

```{r}
tibble(Model = c("A: temp_actual + windspeed + weekend",
                 "C: temp_feel + humidity + weekend"),
       `Adj R2` = c(summary(bikes_A)$adj.r.squared, summary(bikes_C)$adj.r.squared)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

Which model does adjusted $R^2$ prefer? ________________

## Information criteria: AIC and BIC

$$IC = \text{Measure of Fit} + \text{Penalty}$$

$$AIC = n \log(SSE/n) + 2k \qquad\qquad BIC = n \log(SSE/n) + \log(n) \cdot k$$

where $k$ = number of coefficients (**including** the intercept).

-   Smaller values are ______________.
-   When we add a predictor, the fit term gets ______________ and the penalty gets ______________.
-   BIC penalizes more than AIC whenever $\log(n) >$ ______, i.e. $n \ge$ ______.

## By hand

A researcher fits three nested models to $n = 40$ observations. Fill in the
table, then answer the questions. (Use $\log$ = natural log.)

| Model | Predictors | $k$ | SSE | $\hat\sigma^2 = SSE/(n-k)$ | $R^2_{adj}$ | AIC | BIC |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| M0 | none | 1 | 980 | | | | |
| M1 | $x_1$ | 2 | 520 | | | | |
| M2 | $x_1, x_2$ | 3 | 410 | | | | |
| M3 | $x_1, x_2, x_3$ | 4 | 398 | | | | |

$R^2_{adj} = 1 - \hat\sigma^2 / \hat\sigma^2_{M0}$ (since $MST = SSE_{M0}/(n-1)$).

\vspace{2.25in}

**(a)** Which model is best by $R^2_{adj}$? By AIC? By BIC?

\vspace{.5in}

**(b)** Use an $F$-test to compare M2 to M1 and M3 to M2. State $d$ and $df_{full}$ each time.

\vspace{1.5in}

**(c)** Do the tools agree? Explain any disagreement.

## How do the tools relate?

For the `bikes` data ($n = $ `r n_bikes`) and one extra parameter ($d = 1$),
the bigger model is preferred when $F$ is bigger than:

```{r}
df_f <- bikes_A$df.residual
tibble(Rule = c("F-test, alpha = 0.05", "AIC", "BIC"),
       `F needed` = c(qf(0.95, 1, df_f),
                      df_f * (exp(2 / n_bikes) - 1),
                      df_f * (n_bikes^(1 / n_bikes) - 1))) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

**Which is the most willing to add terms?** ________ **Most conservative?** ________

All three ask the same question: ____________________________________________.

## AIC and BIC in R

```{r}
#| echo: true
sse <- sum(residuals(bikes_A)^2)
n <- nrow(bikes)
k <- length(coef(bikes_A))

n * log(sse / n) + 2 * k   # AIC by hand
AIC(bikes_A)               # R's AIC
```

R's value differs from our formula by a constant that is the same for every
model fit to the same data, so ________________________ are identical.

```{r}
mods <- list("A: temp + wind + weekend" = bikes_A,
             "B: A + holiday" = bikes_B,
             "D: B + humidity" = bikes_D,
             "E: D + temp_feel" = bikes_E,
             "C: temp_feel + humidity + weekend" = bikes_C)

tibble(Model = names(mods),
       k = map_int(mods, ~length(coef(.x))),
       `Adj R2` = map_dbl(mods, ~summary(.x)$adj.r.squared),
       AIC = map_dbl(mods, AIC),
       BIC = map_dbl(mods, BIC)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

Summarize what each criterion says about the bikes models:

\vspace{1in}

## Why penalize? Overfitting

```{r}
#| fig-height: 2
#| fig-width: 7.5
set.seed(123)
n <- 30
x <- seq(0, 1, length.out = n)
y <- sin(2 * pi * x) + rnorm(n, sd = 0.3)
df <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)

plot_fit <- function(degree, title) {
  ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
    stat_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ poly(x, degree),
                se = FALSE, color = "#f15a31", linewidth = 1) +
    labs(title = title) +
    theme(axis.title = element_blank(), axis.text = element_blank())
}

plot_fit(1, "Underfit") | plot_fit(3, "Balanced") | plot_fit(15, "Overfit")
```

A model that is too ________________ will do very well on the data used to
fit it but poorly on new data. The penalty in AIC and BIC discourages this.
